The landhopper Arcitalitrus dorrieni is a terrestrial amphipod that has successfully colonized forest floor habitats across parts of Europe and Australasia. Studies on early developmental stages indicate that at a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the incubation period required for the fertilised ovum to develop and hatch is approximately 40.3 days [ab = approximately 40.3 days]. This relatively protracted embryonic phase is characteristic of talitrid amphipods, which produce large, yolk-rich eggs that undergo direct development without a free-swimming larval stage. Upon emergence from the brood pouch, the neonate measures about 0.12 centimeters [Lb = about 0.12 centimeters] in total body length. This diminutive size at birth reflects the constraints of brooding within a confined marsupial space, yet it also marks the onset of an accelerated growth trajectory that will carry the juvenile through several critical developmental transitions in the coming months.

Following the period of maternal incubation, the newly hatched juveniles begin an exotrophic transition, commencing active feeding on decomposing leaf litter and microbial films within the leaf litter layer. Field observations and laboratory rearing experiments have tracked the progressive increase in body dimensions as these individuals approach a key morphological transformation. Larval metamorphosis, which in this species manifests as a post-embryonic allometric shift rather than a discrete larval-juvenile transition, occurs when the growing crustacean attains a total length of 0.3 centimeters . At this threshold, the body plan reorganisation is subtle but functionally significant, involving changes in the relative proportions of the pereiopods and the development of the exoskeletal structures that facilitate more efficient terrestrial locomotion. The achievement of this size landmark is a prerequisite for continued somatic growth and precedes the eventual onset of gonadal maturation.

Reproductive maturation in Arcitalitrus dorrieni follows a predictable pattern governed by cumulative somatic investment. Females typically become reproductively active, entering what is termed the first ovigerous stage, once their total body length reaches approximately 0.81 centimeters [Lp = approximately 0.81 centimeters]. This size at puberty corresponds to a developmental state where the ovaries have completed gametogenesis onset and the individual is capable of sustaining a brood. The ultimate total length that a fully grown adult can achieve under optimal conditions is around 1.47 centimeters [Li = around 1.47 centimeters], a value that is consistent with the asymptotic body size reported for other talitrid amphipods inhabiting temperate forest floors. Attaining this maximum dimension involves several successive moulting events, each incrementally increasing body size, until the individual reaches the final instar stage characteristic of a post-pubertal adult.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the maximum reproductive output of this species has been characterised in detail. Gravid females produce broods with a clutch size of between 59 and 62 eggs [N_R_i = broods with a clutch size of between 59 and 62 eggs] during each successive brooding event. This remarkable fecundity is supported by a high frequency of brooding, with females producing approximately one clutch every day under continuous favourable conditions [F_R_i = approximately one clutch every day under continuous favourable conditions]. The short interval between successive reproductive events is facilitated by the rapid development of oocytes within the paired ovaries and the efficient packing of fertilised ova into the marsupium. These rates, however, are strictly temperature-dependent and are unlikely to be sustained indefinitely in the fluctuating thermal regimes of natural field environments, where resource availability and desiccation risk impose additional constraints on reproductive timing.

In captive populations maintained at a stable temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the oldest documented individuals have survived for a maximum of 730 days [am = 730 days], a duration that encompasses several complete reproductive cycles and permits multiple generations to overlap within the leaf litter microhabitat. This protracted lifespan is accompanied by a maximum adult wet body mass of approximately 40.9 milligrams [Wwi = approximately 40.9 milligrams], a value that reflects the modest size ceiling imposed by the species' terrestrial lifestyle and the mechanical constraints of exoskeletal support. Comparative analyses with other talitrid amphipods, such as the related Arcitalitrus sylvaticus, indicate that this combination of moderate longevity and relatively low adult mass is typical of species occupying stable, resource-rich detritivorous niches in temperate forest ecosystems.
